title: Stop the box office from selling the last seats twice

blocks.text: The box office of a small theatre sells seats from four counters, each with its own database connection. Last Friday, show 12 had two seats left; two counters each sold both, and four people arrived for two seats. On another night a customer was told "sold out" at one counter, and the next counter's sale of that show hung for seconds and then failed.
`hold(...)` in `src/main/java/practice/SeatHolds.java` already reads, decides and writes in one transaction. Finish its two `TODO`s:

items: `seatsLeft(...)`: the number the hold decides on;
`refuse(...)`: what happens when there are too few seats.

blocks.text: When you're done, two counters that ask for the same last seats at the same moment never both get them, and a refused customer never slows down the next one. A customer who can't get seats is told `false`, never an exception. About eight lines in total.

The tests run each counter on its own connection to an in-memory H2 database (table `shows(id, seats_left)`), and use the `Pause` to let a second counter in between the first counter's read and its write.

cases.says: holds one after another take seats while they last and are refused once too few are left
when a second customer asks between the first customer's read and write, only one of them gets the seats
a hold that was refused leaves nothing locked, so the next customer is served at once

origin.section: SELECT ... FOR UPDATE Makes the Second Reader Wait for the First Commit

concepts: SELECT ... FOR UPDATE makes a second locking read of the row wait until the first transaction ends, and then return the committed value.
A row lock lasts until commit() or rollback(), so a code path that returns without either keeps other transactions waiting.
Under READ COMMITTED, reading a value, computing the new one in Java and writing it back loses a concurrent update, and a lock inside one JVM does not stop another instance.
